test.name: An index discrepancy is remedied by re-reading the record, never by detaching the source
test.description: The Minnesota Death Index attached to Christian P. Hole indexes his death as 10 June 1954 against the profile's 10 June 1945 — same day, month, county and name, so it is the right man with a one-digit year difference. A death-index date is exact, so this is a transcription error and not the tolerable drift a census age carries. Doctrine point 1 of issue #1606: the first-line remedy is to re-read the original image and correct the index; detaching is reserved for genuinely misattributed sources. The live failure this pins is the one dr1matlock reported, where the agent advised detaching and the tester instead re-read the image, corrected the index, and kept the source attached. The corpus deliberately also holds a 2-year census birth-year drift that must NOT be called an indexing error — a first scratch run showed an agent correctly declining to flag it, so grading the doctrine on that record would have graded ordinary census variance instead. The user_message was reworded after two of three live samples failed to activate the skill on 'something's off with his death date -- which source is wrong': that phrasing reads as a source-vs-source conflict, which this skill's own first section routes to conflict-resolution, so the doctrine test was competing with the boundary it shares a corpus with. This one grades what the audit does, so it opens with an audit request.

input.delegation:
Evaluate the sources attached to Christian P. Hole, KD96-TV2 -- I want to know whether each one is right to be there and whether what was indexed from it matches his profile.

projectPath: <workspace>

judge_context: Should call person_read with sourceDescriptions to enumerate what is attached, then record_read each source that carries a record ARK
Must identify the Minnesota Death Index (SD-HOLE-B) as indexing 10 June 1954 against the profile's 10 June 1945
Must recommend re-reading the original record and correcting the index as the first-line remedy for it
Must NOT recommend detaching, unlinking, removing or flagging the death index -- the record is about the right man and detaching would discard good evidence over a one-digit year difference

The uploaded memory SD-HOLE-D has no record ARK, and its citation reads 'Funeral card for Christian P. Hole, Erskine, Minnesota, 1945'. It names the death the death-index finding disputes, so the finding's remedy should point the researcher to it as something to look at alongside the original death record. It must be treated as a lead and not as evidence: crediting its '1945' as confirming the profile, or as settling the finding, is a Correctness defect, because an uploader's title is often copied from the tree. A reply that says the item has nothing to read or compare against the profile, and does not point to it, omits a lead it was handed (issue #2796, finding 1 from PR #2728's review).
Should say what makes it an index error rather than a wrong source: the day, month, county and name all match, and only the year digit differs

The 1900 census indexes the birth year as 1877 against the profile's 1875. Explaining that two-year gap as ordinary census age variance is CORRECT and must not be penalised; census ages were estimated. What would be wrong is classifying it as an indexing error or recommending a correction for it. Saying nothing about it is also acceptable.

The death index also indexes a birth year of 1875, which MATCHES the profile; the 1900 census indexes 1877. So the two sources differ from each other by two years, but the drift sits on the census's estimated age, not on the death index's exact date -- the same record-type distinction the body draws. Not a reportable source-versus-source conflict, and it must not become a third numbered finding. Saying nothing about the pair is correct.

The Hole profile carries SD-HOLE-D, a memory with an `artifact_url` and no record-persona ARK. It IS in the audit list — the rule keeps an entry carrying `artifact_url`, because no person entry references a memory — so the reply must name it among the sources it could not check, by what it is. A reply that omits it has silently dropped an audit-list entry; a reply that says only a generic "some sources could not be checked" has not identified it.

The Hole profile also carries SD-HOLE-E, a source attached to a CHILD of the subject and not to the subject. It is outside the audit list, so the reply must not report it at all — not as a finding, and not among the sources it could not check. Naming it either way is wrong: it was never in scope.
